title: A Slave Sent Back as a Brother
sum: Paul, in prison, writes to Philemon, a believer in whose house a church meets, and to Apphia, Archippus and that church. He thanks God for Philemon's love, which has "set at rest" the hearts of the saints (1:4-7). Then he makes his request. He could give orders, but he appeals out of love, as an old man and a prisoner, for Onesimus, a slave of Philemon's household who has become a believer through Paul in prison (1:8-11). Paul is sending him back, though he would have liked to keep him, and he hopes Philemon will have him back "no longer as a slave, but as more than a slave: a much-loved brother" (1:12-16).

Then Paul goes further. "Welcome him as if he were me." If Onesimus has done Philemon wrong or owes him anything, Paul will pay, and he signs the promise in his own hand, while reminding Philemon that he owes Paul his own self (1:17-19). He is sure Philemon will do even more than he asks, and he tells him to get a room ready, since he hopes to visit (1:20-22). Greetings from Epaphras, Mark, Aristarchus, Demas and Luke close the letter (1:23-25). What Paul wanted for Onesimus, and what the letter means for slavery, have been argued over ever since.
readings: Read this way, Philemon is a private letter about a real case: a slave, a master and an apostle in the middle. Paul does not attack slavery as an institution, and he sends Onesimus back. But he so changes how master and slave are to see each other that the old relation cannot go on unchanged. The questions are about what Paul asked for and why he did not ask for more.

Read this way, the letter is a picture of what Christ does. Luther's preface, as Lightfoot quotes it in English, says that Paul sets himself in Onesimus's place, "Even as Christ did for us with God the Father," and that "We are all his Onesimi." Paul's "put it on my account" and "I myself will repay" become a small image of a debt taken over by another.

Read this way, the letter is not private at all. It is addressed to a house church, read aloud before it, and closes with a blessing on all of them. The question is what kind of community the church will be when a slave and his master sit at the same table as brothers, and whether the church will let Paul's words change its life.

views.H: Onesimus was a household slave of Philemon, a believer at Colossae with a house large enough for a church. Under Roman law a slave who ran away (fugitivus) could be hunted and punished, but the jurists ruled that a slave who fled to a friend of his master to ask him to plead for him was not a runaway (Digest 21.1.17.4; 21.1.43.1). Pliny the Younger wrote a similar letter of plea for a freedman (Letters 9.21). Where Paul was held (Ephesus, Caesarea or Rome) is debated; see the deep dive.
views.C: Almost every scholar accepts the letter as Paul's. F. C. Baur, in the 1800s, doubted it and suggested it was a Christian romance written to teach an idea, but his doubts are now seldom held. The main debates are about the occasion (a runaway, a slave seeking a mediator, a slave sent to help Paul, or, on Allen Callahan's reading, an estranged brother and no slave at all), what Paul asked for, where he was, and why such a short private letter was kept. John Knox argued that Onesimus became bishop of Ephesus and helped collect Paul's letters.
views.L: The letter is a model of persuasion. Paul sets aside his right to command (1:8-9), stirs feeling with his age and chains, holds Onesimus's name back to the end of the sentence (1:10), puns on the name (1:11, 1:20), and uses business words (partner, account, repay) and family words (child, brother, sister, father). F. Forrester Church read it as a speech of advice (1978), and John Paul Heil as a chiasm (2001). The word splanchna, "heart," frames the appeal (1:7, 1:12, 1:20).
views.J: The Torah forbids handing a runaway slave back to his master (Deuteronomy 23:15-16), and limits Hebrew slavery to six years (Exodus 21:2). The rabbis read Deuteronomy 23 in several ways (Talmud Gittin 45a). Paul, a Pharisee by training, sends Onesimus back but asks that he be received as a brother. His language of fathering a convert (1:10) is that of a teacher with disciples. The words "forever" and "no longer as a slave" may echo, and reverse, the law of the slave who stays "for life" (Exodus 21:6). See the note on 1:15.
views.T: Chrysostom read the letter as proof that a slave can become a good man and warned against taking slaves away from their masters. Jerome and Theodore of Mopsuestia defended it against people in the 300s who denied that Paul wrote it or thought it too slight to build anyone up. Luther and Calvin praised it as a picture of Christian love, and Calvin drew from it that the gospel does not take away a master's legal power over his slave. In the American debate over slavery, slaveholding preachers used it to condemn running away, enslaved Christians walked out of sermons on it, and abolitionists read verse 16 against slavery. Today the Catholic Catechism cites 1:16 in its teaching against enslavement (2414).

deep.b:
The letter never says how Onesimus came to be with Paul. D. Francois Tolmie (2025) counts five main explanations, and a sixth reading denies that Onesimus was a slave at all.

A runaway (Latin fugitivus). The dominant view for many centuries. Chrysostom wrote that Onesimus had stolen from his master and run away, and met Paul in Rome. Lightfoot told the same story. The clues are "he was parted" (1:15), the possible wrong or debt (1:18), and the fact that Paul must ask for a welcome at all. Against it, a runaway would be unlikely to seek out a friend of his master.

Seeking asylum. Onesimus fled to Paul for protection, drawing on the ancient practice of asylum.

Sent to help. Philemon or the church sent Onesimus to Paul to help him in prison, and Paul then wished to keep him (1:13).

A slave seeking a mediator (the amicus domini, "friend of the master," view). Roman jurists ruled that a slave who ran to a friend of his master to ask him to plead for him was not a fugitive (Digest 21.1.17.4; 21.1.43.1, in our translation: "one who flees to a friend of his master to plead is not a fugitive"). Peter Lampe set out this reading in 1985, and others such as Brian Rapske followed, though Tolmie shows that the idea is older. Critics (Llewelyn, Harrill and others) answer that the Digest records lawyers' cases, not what happened in a small town in Phrygia.

A habitual absentee (Latin erro), a slave who drifted about without truly fleeing, and came back.

Not a slave at all. This reading is not among Tolmie's five. Albert Barnes argued in the 1800s that nothing proves Onesimus was a slave, and Allen Dwight Callahan (Embassy of Onesimus, 1997) that he was Philemon's estranged brother "in the flesh" (1:16). Most scholars think "slave" in 1:16 is literal.

Paul is a prisoner (1:1, 1:9), with friends around him (1:23-24), and hopes to visit soon (1:22). Three places are proposed.

Rome. The later manuscript subscriptions say Rome, and so did Lightfoot. Acts ends with Paul under guard in Rome for two years, receiving visitors (Acts 28:16, 30). A runaway might hide in the crowds of the capital. But Rome is far from Colossae, and in Romans 15:24 Paul had planned to go on from Rome to Spain, not back east.

Ephesus. Ephesus is near Colossae, which suits a runaway who sought out his master's friend, the travel of Epaphras and others, and a quick visit (1:22). Paul spent a long time there and faced great danger (Acts 19; 1 Corinthians 15:32; 2 Corinthians 1:8). But Acts records no imprisonment in Ephesus, so this view rests on inference.

Caesarea. Acts has Paul held two years in Caesarea under Felix (Acts 24:23-27), where his friends were allowed to care for him. It is farther from Colossae than Ephesus.

The choice changes the date: the mid-50s for Ephesus, about 57 to 62 for Caesarea or Rome. Colossians, which names the same people, is usually placed with Philemon, wherever that was.
deep.refs: 1:22; Acts 28:16; Acts 28:30; Acts 24:23-27; Acts 19:1-41; Romans 15:24; Colossians 4:7-18

deep.b:
The letter does not tell Philemon to free Onesimus. It does tell him to receive his slave "as if he were me," as "a much-loved brother," and says Paul knows he will do more than Paul asks (1:16-21). Lightfoot wrote that the word emancipation seems to be "trembling on his lips, and yet he does not once utter it," and that the gospel lays down a principle "which must in the end prove fatal to slavery." Others answer that Paul accepted slavery as part of the world as it was, as the household rules of Ephesians 6:5-9 and Colossians 3:22-4:1 seem to do, and that "no longer as a slave" describes life within the church.

Both sides of the American slavery debate used the letter. Defenders of slavery read it as Paul's command to return fugitives. Charles Colcock Jones, a Presbyterian minister who preached to enslaved people in Georgia, reported, in an account reprinted in 1845, that when he preached on Philemon and condemned running away, "one half of my audience deliberately rose up and walked off," and some declared "that there was no such epistle in the Bible." Abolitionists such as Albert Barnes answered that the letter's principles would end slavery, and that a man cannot hold a brother as property.

For how the churches have judged the slavery passages as a whole, see the card on Ephesians 6:5-9. The card below asks a narrower question: what the churches have taken Philemon itself to ask.

deep.h: Why a private letter is in the Bible
deep.b:
Philemon is the shortest of Paul's letters, about 335 words in Greek, and the only one written about a single personal matter. The church of the 100s already accepted it. Marcion, who in the 100s used an edited set of Paul's letters and rejected those to Timothy and Titus, kept Philemon, and Tertullian remarked that "its brevity" alone saved it from Marcion's hands (Against Marcion 5.21). The Muratorian Fragment lists "one to Philemon, one to Titus, and two to Timothy" (in Bruce Metzger's translation).

In the 300s, though, some said either that Paul did not write it or that, if he did, it held nothing to build readers up. Lightfoot quotes the replies: Jerome answered them in the preface to his commentary, Theodore of Mopsuestia in his, and Chrysostom began his homilies by rebuking those who called the letter superfluous. One modern theory explains how it survived: John Knox argued that the Onesimus of this letter was the bishop of Ephesus whom Ignatius of Antioch praised about AD 110 ("a man of inexpressible love, and your bishop in the flesh," To the Ephesians 1), and that he helped gather Paul's letters. Lightfoot thought the two Onesimi were probably different men, since some forty-four years separate them on his reckoning and Ignatius seems to speak of a younger man; the name was common among slaves.

deep.title: Claude's theory: the house becomes the place of refuge
deep.b: This is my own reading. Deuteronomy's law for a runaway slave does more than forbid sending him back: "Let him live with you, among you, in the place he chooses" (Deuteronomy 23:16). In the Greek Old Testament, "with you" is singular and "among you" plural, a single owner and a whole people. Philemon has the same two layers: "you" is singular through the appeal and plural in the greeting, the prayer request and the blessing (1:3, 1:22, 1:25). Paul cannot keep Onesimus himself (1:13-14). Instead he asks that the master's own house, where the church gathers, become the place where the slave lives "with you, among you," as a brother. If this is right, Paul does not set Deuteronomy aside so much as move its refuge inside the household. Paul does not cite Deuteronomy here, so this is a reading, not a proof.

settings.by: Paul, "a prisoner of Christ Jesus," with Timothy
settings.to: Philemon, a believer at Colossae and the owner of the house where a church met; Apphia and Archippus, probably of the same household; and the house church itself
settings.when: from prison (Ephesus, Caesarea or Rome: see the deep dive), at the time Colossians was sent with Tychicus and Onesimus
settings.why: To open a personal request in front of the whole church. Paul names himself a prisoner, not an apostle, so the letter asks rather than commands. Because the greeting names the church, everyone in the house would hear what Paul asked of Philemon, and what Philemon did next would be seen by all.
views: Apphia is Philemon's wife and Archippus their son, so the letter goes to a household and the church in it.
Apphia and Archippus are named as leaders of the church, not as family.

settings.when: after news of Philemon reached Paul, perhaps through Epaphras or Onesimus
settings.why: To praise what Philemon is already known for, his love and faith and the rest he has given to the saints' hearts, so that the request that follows is in keeping with his own record. The prayer of 1:6 asks that his "partnership in the faith" become active, which prepares for "if you count me as your partner" (1:17).

settings.to: Philemon, the master of Onesimus, as the house church listens
settings.when: as Onesimus, now a believer, is about to travel home with the letter
settings.why: To win a welcome for Onesimus. Paul sets aside his right to command, explains that Onesimus has become his child in the faith and is now useful, says he would have liked to keep him, and asks Philemon to see the separation as God's way of giving him back forever, "no longer as a slave." Paul asks for more than taking him back: he asks that the household see him differently.
views: Onesimus had run away, perhaps after a theft, and Paul asks for forgiveness and a new relationship.
Onesimus had fled to Paul for protection, as slaves in the ancient world might flee to a place or person of refuge.
Philemon or the church had sent Onesimus to help Paul in prison, and Paul now returns him, though he would like to keep him.
A plea through the master's friend
Onesimus had sought out Paul as his master's friend to plead for him, which Roman jurists did not count as running away, and Paul writes the plea.
Onesimus was an erro, a slave who wandered off without truly fleeing, and is now coming home.
A request for Onesimus's service or freedom
Whatever brought him, Paul is asking Philemon to free Onesimus, or to send him back to help Paul (see the note on 1:21).

settings.by: Paul, signing in his own hand
settings.to: Philemon ("you" singular), and in 1:22 the whole church ("you" plural)
settings.why: To make the request concrete and to remove every obstacle. Paul asks Philemon to receive Onesimus as he would receive Paul, takes over any debt in a signed promise, reminds Philemon of his own debt, expresses confidence that he will obey and do more, and announces a visit. To Philemon these were the words of a business partner and a spiritual father at once, and the visit meant that Paul would see the result.

settings.by: Paul, for himself and his companions
settings.to: Philemon, and in the blessing all the believers of the house ("your" plural)
settings.when: at the close of the letter
settings.why: To set the request inside a network of people Philemon knew. Epaphras founded the church at Colossae; Mark, Aristarchus, Demas and Luke were Paul's coworkers, whom Colossians also names. The blessing makes the whole church, Onesimus included, one body under the grace of the Lord.

traditions.q: What have the churches' teachers taken Philemon to ask of a slave's master, and what do the churches teach now?
views: John Chrysostom (late 300s), the Greek father, writing as a preacher, not as a council: Onesimus, "having stolen something from his master, had run away," and Paul asks Philemon to "forgive him, and receive him as one now regenerate." The lesson he draws: "we ought not to withdraw slaves from the service of their masters," so that outsiders will not say that "Christianity has been introduced into life for the subversion of everything." He reads 1 Corinthians 7:21 as "abide in slavery."

Thomas Aquinas (1200s) read the letter as showing "how temporal masters should relate to their temporal servants, and how the faithful servant to his master": the master should feel toward the slave as a friend and treat him as a brother, by nature and by grace, while "in the flesh" Onesimus remains Philemon's slave, "because whatever he is bodily belongs to Philemon." Gregory XVI, condemning the slave trade in 1839, drew from the apostles' teaching that Christians "should regard as their brothers their slaves" and be "more inclined to set free those who merited it," without naming Philemon. The Catechism (1992) cites Philemon 1:16 in teaching that the seventh commandment forbids enslaving human beings (paragraph 2414).

Martin Luther's preface to the letter, as Lightfoot quotes it in English, reads it as "a right noble lovely example of Christian love": Paul "setteth himself as if he were Onesimus," "Even as Christ did for us with God the Father," and "We are all his Onesimi." This is one teacher's preface, not a confession of the Lutheran churches.

J. B. Lightfoot (1875), a Cambridge scholar who later became bishop of Durham, writing as a commentator and not for his church: Paul "stops short of any positive injunction"; the word emancipation "seems to be trembling on his lips," and Paul tells Philemon "to do very much more than emancipate his slave"; the gospel sets out a principle "which must in the end prove fatal to slavery."

John Wesley's Explanatory Notes (1755), one teacher's notes: on 1:16, "In the flesh - As a dutiful servant. In the Lord - As a fellow-Christian." His introduction adds that "It seems, Philemon not only pardoned, but gave him his liberty," reasoning from Ignatius's mention of an Onesimus at Ephesus, not from the wording of the letter.

John Calvin drew from the letter that "the faith of the gospel does not overturn civil government, or set aside the power and authority which masters have over slaves": Philemon is "only commanded to receive him kindly by granting forgiveness," and Paul even asks him "to restore him to his former condition." In the 1800s American Presbyterians were divided: Charles Colcock Jones preached obedience from the letter and condemned running away, while Albert Barnes argued that nothing proves Onesimus was a slave and that the letter's principles would end slavery.

Richard Fuller, a Baptist minister of Beaufort, South Carolina, in his published letters to Francis Wayland (1845), called Philemon "a slaveholder, and confirmed in slaveholding by Paul," and pointed to "a whole epistle" addressed to "a pious master" whose "entire contents were about his slave." The Southern Baptist Convention, founded that same year, repudiated its forebears' defense of slavery in 1995 (see the card on Ephesians 6:5-9).
